title: Causal Inference in Clinical Medical Research
text:
Preface
Causal inference is a central scientific approach to studying cause-and-effect relationships: its core aim is to determine whether a cause produces an effect and how large that effect is. This book systematically introduces causal-inference methods for contemporary clinical medical research, spanning randomized controlled trials; real-world study designs based on propensity scores, instrumental variables, regression discontinuity, and time-series analysis; and machine-learning- and AI-driven causal inference.
The book is intended as an advanced text in medical statistics for medical students, clinical researchers, and researchers in statistics and artificial intelligence.

title: 1  Framework for Causal Inference
text:
1.1 Individual Causal Effects
Zhang San is a patient with intracerebral hemorrhage. On October 1, he underwent surgery for an acute hemorrhage and was alive one month later. Imagine that he had not received surgery on October 1: he might have died within the following month. With this information, most people would agree that surgery saved Zhang San’s life. Surgery therefore had a causal effect on his one-month survival.
Another patient, Li Si, also experienced intracerebral hemorrhage on October 1. He did not undergo surgery and died one month later. We may imagine that, had Li Si received surgery on October 1, he might have survived. Surgery therefore could also have had a causal effect on Li Si’s one-month survival.
These examples illustrate causal reasoning: we compare the outcome when an action is taken with the outcome when it is not taken, even though the latter comparison is usually only imagined. If the two outcomes differ, the action has a causal effect on the outcome; otherwise, it does not. In epidemiology, statistics, economics, and other social sciences, such an action is often called an intervention, exposure, or treatment.
To express this intuition mathematically, consider a binary treatment variable—common in clinical research—where \(T=1\) denotes treatment and \(T=0\) denotes no treatment or control, and a binary outcome where \(Y=1\) denotes death and \(Y=0\) denotes survival. The outcome under treatment is written as:
Equation 1.1 Potential outcome under treatment
\[Y^{T=1}\]
The outcome without treatment is written as:
Equation 1.2 Potential outcome without treatment
\[Y^{T=0}\]
For Zhang San or Li Si, the causal effect is:
Equation 1.3 Individual causal effect
\[Y^{T=1}-Y^{T=0}\]
If this difference is zero, treatment has no causal effect for that person; if it is nonzero, treatment has a causal effect. Because this effect applies to Zhang San or Li Si specifically, it is called an individual causal effect.
The two examples require us to imagine the treatment opposite to the one actually received: what would have happened if Zhang San had not undergone surgery, or if Li Si had undergone surgery? The alternative to what actually happened is called a potential outcome; it is also called a counterfactual outcome to emphasize that it represents a situation that did not occur. In almost all settings, however, only one potential outcome can be observed for each person. We know that Zhang San had surgery and survived, and that Li Si did not have surgery and died; the other potential outcome is unobserved. In this sense, an individual causal effect is not identifiable. This framework is known as the potential-outcomes or counterfactual framework. It can be traced to Neyman’s 1923 analysis of randomized experiments and Rubin’s 1974 extension to observational studies, and is therefore also called the Neyman–Rubin potential-outcomes model. Holland (1986) described the fact that each individual can contribute at most one observed potential outcome as the fundamental problem of causal inference.

1.2 Causation and Association
A well-known statistical maxim is that “association does not imply causation.” Ice-cream sales are associated with attendance at swimming pools. It is easy to see why they move together, but we would not say that higher ice-cream sales cause more people to visit swimming pools, or vice versa. In ordinary circumstances, hot weather increases ice-cream sales and also encourages people to go swimming. Both variables share a common cause: warm weather. This idea is discussed in detail in Chapter 8.
Case 1.1
Suppose that the emergency neurosurgery department at Huashan Hospital, Fudan University, admitted 10 patients with intracerebral hemorrhage (Table 1.1). Five underwent surgery and five received non-surgical treatment. Mortality was lower among surgical patients (1/5, 20%) than among patients managed conservatively (3/5, 60%). We can therefore say that surgery is associated with mortality, and it is easy to make the erroneous inference that surgery reduces mortality in intracerebral hemorrhage. Yet we do not know whether the surgical patients would also have survived without surgery, or whether surgery could have saved the lives of those who did not receive it. If conservatively managed patients were too severely ill to tolerate surgery, the association is unsurprising.

If these treatments were to be introduced in China, which would be preferable? Overall, treatment A appears preferable because its response rate is 70%, compared with 60% for treatment B. Yet within both mild and severe disease, treatment B has the higher response rate: 90% versus 80% in mild disease, and 50% versus 20% in severe disease.
The apparent paradox arises because looking only at the “overall” column favors A, whereas considering both severity strata favors B. Which treatment should be chosen?
Usually, treatment B should be chosen. Both common sense and the data indicate that response rates are higher in mild than in severe disease. Most mildly ill patients received A (1,000 received A and 100 received B), whereas most severely ill patients received B (300 received B and 200 received A). In other words, A’s higher overall response rate reflects the fact that A was used mainly in mildly ill patients. Disease severity confounds the relationship between treatment and response. To correct this confounding, treatment and outcome must be compared within severity strata. This leads to choosing treatment B.
There is, however, a less common possibility. Treatment B might be so scarce that patients must wait a long time to receive it, while A is immediately available. Because COVID-19 pneumonia can progress over time, waiting for B could allow mildly ill patients to become severely ill and reduce B’s overall response rate. Thus, even if B is more effective within each severity stratum, choosing B might worsen the overall outcome if access to it causes harmful delay.
This example shows that surface associations alone do not guide treatment decisions. Understanding the underlying causal relationships is necessary to resolve Simpson’s paradox and to guide clinical and public-health decisions.

section: 1.5 Conditions for Estimating an Average Causal Effect
text:
1.5 Conditions for Estimating an Average Causal Effect
The preceding section defined the average causal effect in a hypothetical setting in which every patient receives surgery and in another setting in which every patient receives no surgery. In reality, we cannot observe both potential outcomes for the same patient; we only have the first three columns of Table 1.3. As discussed above, directly comparing mortality in surgical and conservatively managed patients yields an association. Under what conditions can that association be interpreted as an average causal effect?
Four conditions are required.

Exchangeability. We cannot directly compare surgical and conservatively managed patients because the groups may not be comparable. Imagine the surgical patients as an original file and the non-surgical patients as copy-and-paste duplicates of that file: intuitively, the two groups would then be comparable because they would be identical in all respects other than treatment. If either the original or its duplicate received surgery, its outcome would be the same; the same would hold if either received conservative treatment. This is exchangeability. Complete exchangeability is generally unrealistic in observed data, because the two groups are rarely identical in every characteristic other than treatment. Randomized controlled trials can make the assumption more plausible, as discussed in the next chapter.
Conditional exchangeability. Complete exchangeability is unrealistic in observational data, but exchangeability may hold after conditioning on relevant variables. In the example in Section 3, one may control for disease severity by comparing the response rates of treatments A and B only among patients with mild COVID-19 pneumonia. Although response rates may be related to severity overall, within the mild stratum they are no longer compared across different severity levels. Controlling for severity can therefore produce conditional exchangeability between treatment groups.
Conditional exchangeability, also called no unmeasured confounding, is a central causal-inference assumption. It is more realistic than complete exchangeability, but it cannot usually be verified: unmeasured confounders may be absent from the data. Intuitively, the best practical approach is to observe and record as many relevant variables as possible.
Positivity (overlap). When comparing surgery with conservative treatment for intracerebral hemorrhage, there must be patients who receive surgery and patients who receive conservative treatment. If everyone receives surgery, the average causal effect cannot be estimated. Positivity is also required within relevant subgroups. For example, patients with hematoma volumes below 10 mL generally do not undergo surgery; in that group, the average causal effect of surgery versus no surgery cannot be learned from the data (and may not be clinically necessary). In other words, the covariate distributions of the treatment and control groups must overlap, so that every subgroup relevant to the comparison has some probability of receiving each treatment.
Consistency. Return to surgery for intracerebral hemorrhage. Defining treatment merely as “surgery” or “no surgery” may be too vague to satisfy consistency. Surgery may include craniotomy with hematoma evacuation, burr-hole drainage, or intracranial-pressure monitoring; it may also depend on the surgeon and on whether conventional microscopic or newer endoscopic techniques are used. Causal inference therefore requires a precise definition of treatment, including its mode, method, dose, and timing. This requirement is closely related to Rubin’s stable unit treatment value assumption (SUTVA): an individual’s potential outcome is not affected by treatments received by others (no interference), and each treatment corresponds to one well-defined version. Exchangeability, conditional exchangeability, positivity, and consistency are identification conditions that allow associations to be interpreted as causal effects. Hernán and Robins (2020) discuss them systematically; the epidemiologic formulation of exchangeability can be traced to Greenland and Robins (1986), and Cole and Frangakis (2009) discuss the precise meaning of consistency.

Case 1.3
One study question concerns postmenopausal hormone therapy and cardiovascular events. Consider two studies: an observational study and a randomized controlled trial. In the randomized trial, 16,000 menopausal women were randomly assigned to initiate hormone therapy or not to use hormones. The published results suggested that initiating hormones increased the risk of cardiovascular events by 20%, with a hazard ratio of 1.24.
In an observational study, women currently using hormones had a 30% lower risk of cardiovascular events than women who had never used hormones, with a hazard ratio of 0.68.
The results appear contradictory, and randomized trials are generally considered more reliable. Why did the studies differ? The interventions of interest were different. The observational study compared women currently using hormones with women who had never used them; the randomized trial compared initiating hormones with not initiating hormones. Thus, the causal question in the observational study was not the causal question in the randomized trial.
Reanalysis of the randomized-trial results shows that, during the first two years after hormone initiation, cardiovascular-event risk was indeed increased. With more than five years of follow-up, however, cardiovascular-event risk was lower among these women. Participants who experienced cardiovascular events early had already reached the outcome and were no longer under follow-up; women remaining at later times were inherently less likely to experience such events. The observational study had a similar problem, because hormone users who experienced cardiovascular events could not enter the comparison as current users, producing an apparently protective association.
When the observational study was reanalyzed by restricting the comparison to initiators and non-initiators, its conclusion agreed with that of the randomized trial: women initiating hormones had increased cardiovascular risk. This illustrates why defining the causal question is essential.
The two studies in Case 1.3 are the classic analysis of Hernán et al. (2008). When investigators designed and analyzed the observational Nurses’ Health Study to emulate the randomized Women’s Health Initiative (WHI), and allowed risk to vary with time since hormone initiation, the results became more consistent. This illustrates target-trial emulation: first specify the hypothetical randomized trial to be emulated, then use observational data to emulate it, thereby avoiding design biases such as inappropriate inclusion of prevalent users (Hernán and Robins, 2016).

title: 2  Randomized Controlled Trials
text:
2.1 The magic of randomization
Intuitively, randomization is like tossing a coin. A patient with intracerebral hemorrhage receives surgery if the coin lands heads and conservative treatment if it lands tails. Under randomization, the risk of death arising from the patient’s own characteristics is the same in either treatment group: the probability of receiving surgery is unrelated to those characteristics. Likewise, the risk of death caused by every factor other than treatment is the same in either group: the probability of receiving surgery is unrelated to any other factor. Formally, the groups are said to be exchangeable. Exchangeability means that the risk of death under surgery is the same for the heads and tails groups, as is the risk of death under conservative treatment. Equivalently, potential outcomes and treatment are independent. In the language of Chapter 1, randomization ensures exchangeability between groups in expectation and thereby supports the exchangeability, positivity, and other conditions required to identify causal effects. This is the fundamental reason randomized controlled trials are regarded as the gold standard for causal inference.

title: 2  Randomized Controlled Trials
text:
2.2 Common randomized controlled trial designs

2.2.1 Parallel-group design
This is the most commonly used RCT design. Eligible participants are randomly assigned to an experimental or control group and then receive the corresponding intervention. The two groups are observed in the same environment, and investigators use objective outcome measures to assess the effect. The allocation ratio is most often 1:1, although the experimental group may be assigned a larger share when prior non-randomized evidence suggests that it may provide substantially greater benefit.


2.2.2 Cluster-randomized design
Cluster designs are mainly used when it is unsuitable to randomize individuals. If trial participants share a ward, hospital, or community, individual allocation can easily blur the distinction between intervention and non-intervention. A cluster RCT therefore randomizes entire wards, hospitals, or communities, which then receive the intervention or control condition. Apart from the unit being randomized, its design and requirements are similar to a parallel RCT. Cluster trials generally require much larger sample sizes, and the number of clusters and within-cluster correlation must be specified in advance.


2.2.3 Crossover randomized trial
Unlike an ordinary RCT, a crossover trial has two periods. In the first period group A receives the experimental treatment and group B the control; in the second period the treatments are exchanged. A washout period is placed between periods to eliminate effects of the first treatment. This design can mitigate the ethical concern that the control group is denied an effective treatment and, in one sense, increases the information contributed by each participant.


2.2.4 Stepped-wedge randomized trial
A stepped-wedge design is most often used for cluster RCTs. Participants are divided into and label several groups (for example A, B, C, D, E, and F). Before the study begins, the number of groups starting the intervention at each step (for example two) and the time interval (for example three months) are specified. The first two groups in the predetermined order receive the intervention, while the remaining groups wait as controls. Three months later the next two groups begin the intervention, and three months after that the final two groups do so. Over time every group receives the intervention and the study ends. This design substantially reduces the ethical burden, maximizes participant benefit, and retains both randomization and control. It cannot usually be double-blind: at most the outcome assessor can be blinded. Delayed intervention effects require careful consideration and an appropriate step length.

title: 2  Randomized Controlled Trials
text:
2.3 Randomization methods

2.3.1 Simple randomization
Simple randomization is the most basic form. A coin toss can assign a participant to group A when heads occurs and group B when tails occurs. In clinical research, a random-number table may also be used: select a row or column of digits arranged at random, assigning odd numbers to A and even numbers to B. Its main advantage is ease of implementation. Its main disadvantage is that small samples may be markedly unbalanced between groups, reducing power to detect a true difference. For example, with 20 participants, the probability that the group ratio lies between 12:8 and 8:12 is about 50%.
An incorrect alternative is alternating allocation (for example, ABABAB…). This is not random. Except for the first participant, investigators and participants know the upcoming assignment, which can introduce bias. Preventing investigators and participants from knowing the forthcoming group is called allocation concealment. Allocation concealment and blinding are different concepts: concealment keeps the allocation sequence unknown before assignment to prevent selective enrollment; blinding keeps participants, investigators, or assessors unaware of the assigned group after assignment. Both are essential means of reducing bias (Schulz and Grimes 2002). The design and reporting of RCTs can follow the CONSORT statement (Schulz et al. 2010).


2.3.2 Block randomization
Block randomization avoids the imbalance that can arise with simple randomization. First choose a block size, for example four. Of the first four enrolled participants, randomly assign half to A and half to B; repeat this process for each succeeding block until all participants are randomized. A potential drawback is that, when block size is known and the trial is not double-blind, the final one or two assignments in a block may be predictable. With blocks of four, for example, after BAA the final assignment must be B; after BB the remaining two must be AA. This can be avoided by varying the block size, randomly choosing among sizes such as 2, 4, 6, and 8 after each completed block.


2.3.3 Stratified randomization
Some baseline characteristics are related to outcome; age, for example, is prognostic in many studies. Simple randomization may distribute prognostic factors unevenly between treatment and control groups. Stratified randomization helps make such factors comparable across groups. Each factor is divided into two or more subgroups (for example, male/female); the total number of strata is the product of the numbers of subgroups for all factors, and randomization is carried out within the stratum to which a participant belongs. In multicenter RCTs, center may be an important prognostic factor and should be used for stratification.

title: 2  Randomized Controlled Trials
text:
2.4 Blinding

2.4.1 Open-label trials
Open-label studies are usually easier and less costly to conduct, but their principal disadvantage is the possibility of bias. This is particularly important when outcomes depend on self-report or symptom assessment: both efficacy and safety reporting may be biased. Participants receiving a drug may exaggerate benefit because they believe it works, or exaggerate adverse effects because they fear them. Participants who expect benefit but are assigned to control may be dissatisfied and withdraw. Investigators may also introduce bias. In a trial of coronary artery bypass surgery versus medical treatment, the two groups had the same number of smokers at baseline, but smokers in the surgical group decreased markedly early in follow-up. A possible explanation is that unblinded surgeons gave more advice not to smoke to participants who underwent surgery.


2.4.2 Single-blind trials
In a single-blind study only the participants do not know which intervention they receive. Its disadvantages resemble those of an open-label design. Investigators often prefer positive results, which may be more likely to appear in high-impact journals and bring conference invitations or funding. They may therefore unconsciously favor the intervention group while collecting data or evaluating and interpreting results. Concomitant treatments—any non-study treatment provided during the trial—can also introduce bias if they are used unequally between groups.


2.4.3 Double-blind trials
In a double-blind study, neither participants nor investigators collecting data and assessing outcomes know the intervention assignment. This design is generally limited to trials of drugs or biological products and is rarely feasible for surgical RCTs. Its principal advantage is a reduced risk of bias. In drug trials requiring dose adjustment through monitoring adverse effects, an unblinded pharmacist or clinician independent of the investigators may perform the adjustment.

title: 2  Randomized Controlled Trials
text:
2.5 Noninferiority trials
A noninferiority trial tests whether one intervention is not worse than another. A conventional superiority trial tests whether two interventions differ in efficacy. In a noninferiority trial, intervention A may be better than B, the same as B, or somewhat worse than B, provided that the difference does not exceed the noninferiority margin.
Case 2.1
Warfarin is commonly used for patients with atrial fibrillation, and several randomized trials have shown that it reduces ischemic stroke risk. Its adverse effect is bleeding. Suppose a new drug may be more effective and cause fewer adverse effects than warfarin; ignoring price, it would clearly be preferred. Even if it has the same efficacy but fewer adverse effects, it would still be preferred. Thus, even if superiority cannot be shown, use of the new drug is reasonable if it can be shown not to be worse than warfarin. A noninferiority trial can therefore compare their efficacy.
The key concept is the noninferiority margin. Assume that the odds ratio measures the effectiveness of the new drug versus warfarin. In a superiority trial, the 95% confidence interval for the odds ratio must lie below 1. In a noninferiority trial, an odds ratio of 1 is acceptable because it indicates that the new drug is not inferior. A threshold—the noninferiority margin—must be specified in advance, and the upper limit of the 95% confidence interval must fall below it for the new drug to be considered noninferior. The margin should be set at the design stage using efficacy established in prior placebo-controlled trials, usually retaining a specified proportion of the observed effect (the effect-retention approach); it must not be relaxed merely to improve power. The CONSORT extension provides guidance for design and reporting of noninferiority and equivalence trials (Piaggio et al. 2012).


Figure 2.1 Illustration of the noninferiority margin.

In Figure 2.1, the horizontal axis is the odds ratio. The blue dashed line at 1 is the null hypothesis for a superiority trial. An estimated odds ratio below 1 favors the new drug because the risk is lower. The red dashed line just to the right of 1 is the noninferiority margin: it represents a small, clinically unimportant disadvantage of the new drug that remains acceptable. A–F represent point estimates (the letter positions) and 95% confidence intervals (the line lengths) from six hypothetical trials.
In trial A, both the point estimate and the 95% confidence interval lie entirely below 1, indicating superiority of the new treatment. In trial B, the point estimate is below 1 but the 95% confidence interval includes 1; superiority cannot be claimed. However, the entire interval is below the noninferiority margin, so the new drug is noninferior. Trial C is likewise noninferior because the upper confidence limit is below the margin. Trial D fails noninferiority because its upper confidence limit exceeds the margin; indeed, its entire interval favors warfarin, indicating superiority of warfarin. Trial E indicates that the new drug is much worse than warfarin. Trial F has a very wide confidence interval and supports neither superiority nor noninferiority.

title: 2  Randomized Controlled Trials
text:
2.6 Pragmatic clinical trials
Conventional clinical trials are often optimized: experienced research staff participate and highly selected participants are enrolled. They may overestimate benefit, underestimate harm, and be difficult to translate into practice. Pragmatic RCTs commonly ask whether a health policy or medical decision can improve participant outcomes. They seek to simulate usual care and have goals close to the real world. The distinction between pragmatic and explanatory trials was introduced by Schwartz and Lellouch (1967): pragmatic trials focus on effectiveness in usual care, whereas explanatory trials focus on efficacy under ideal conditions. The PRECIS-2 tool can be used to assess pragmatism across eligibility, follow-up, adherence, and other design domains (Loudon et al. 2015).

2.6.1 Low complexity
Pragmatic trials minimize inclusion and exclusion criteria and reduce the number and complexity of follow-up visits, thereby increasing participation.


2.6.2 Consent may be waived in special circumstances
With ethics approval, trials may sometimes proceed without informed consent. In the CRASH trial, more than 10,000 patients with head injury and impaired consciousness were randomized to determine whether corticosteroids affected mortality and neurologic disability compared with placebo. Because treatment had to be given very soon after injury, risk was considered minimal, usual care was not disrupted, and no extra follow-up was added, the investigators sought an ethics waiver of consent. The Declaration of Helsinki states that research may proceed without consent when it cannot be obtained and the research cannot be delayed.


2.6.3 Blinding is usually not used
Blinded trials are not fully pragmatic, since treatments in routine practice are explicit. Allocation is therefore usually unmasked. To minimize bias, primary outcomes are commonly objectively assessable major events such as death or emergency admission.


2.6.4 No additional follow-up
Follow-up in pragmatic research should not add burden to participants or staff, and no extra visits are required. This approach is most feasible in health systems with reliable, accessible electronic health records that capture events of interest.


2.6.5 Assessment of adherence
Pragmatic research does not require every participant to complete the assigned regimen. Adherence itself can be analyzed as an outcome; poor adherence suggests that the treatment is not feasible in real-world practice.


2.6.6 Outcome ascertainment and analysis
Pragmatic outcomes are usually simple to minimize data-collection requirements. The CRASH trial achieved considerable simplification with a two-page case-report form. In another catheter trial, the primary outcome was symptomatic catheter-associated urinary tract infection within six weeks after discharge rather than laboratory-confirmed in-hospital infection. Mail questionnaires or web-based forms are often used instead of clinic visits, substantially reducing cost.

title: 2  Randomized Controlled Trials
text:
2.7 Adaptive clinical trials
An adaptive clinical trial uses information accumulated within and outside the trial to modify specified aspects of its design dynamically according to prespecified rules, without undermining validity, scientific rigor, or integrity. Modifications may include allocation ratios, total sample size, and eligibility criteria; a trial may extend from phase II to phase III or add or drop treatment arms. Adaptive designs may shorten completion time, reduce resource requirements and exposure to ineffective treatments, and improve the overall probability of success.
Common adaptive designs include sample-size re-estimation, response-adaptive randomization, dropping futile arms, adaptive enrichment, and seamless phase II–III designs. Sample size may be re-estimated using the observed event rate and actual power during the trial. Response-adaptive randomization changes allocation probabilities during the trial, so participants enrolled after favorable interim results are more likely to receive the intervention. Adaptive enrichment modifies eligibility or outcome assessment: when interim analysis indicates a favorable response in a subgroup, eligibility can be modified to recruit only or mainly that subgroup. Seamless designs continue from one phase to the next, typically phase II to phase III; phase II results can determine initial allocation ratios and planned total sample size, while phase III expands to a larger population.
Adaptive RCTs retain the principle of randomization and still require a sample-size calculation, but prespecified rules determine the next-stage sample size as the study proceeds. Conventional frequentist methods may not predict adjustments to individual treatment assignment well; Bayesian methods may therefore use prior information to predict treatment performance. Adaptive designs rely heavily on computer simulation. Investigators and trial statisticians must be convinced that expected benefits—fewer required participants, shorter completion, and fewer ineffective treatments—outweigh potential risks such as unstable interim effect estimates and reduced robustness of final analyses. Implementation usually involves repeated interim-analysis and decision cycles. Rules specified before the trial begins include mathematical criteria for stopping an arm or trial, changes in allocation ratios, sample-size re-estimation, narrowing eligibility, and selection of new arms.
The statistical analysis plan for an adaptive design includes simulations, interim analyses, and final analysis of the completed trial. A run-in period is needed, during which a prespecified number of patients may be enrolled at a fixed allocation ratio (usually 1:1) to ensure sufficient data and reasonable precision. Adaptation too early is vulnerable to random error from sparse data. A rule of thumb for response-adaptive randomization is to conduct the first interim analysis after at least 20–30 participants per group. Other adaptations, including sample-size re-estimation and enrichment, usually need a longer run-in and larger sample. In multi-arm adaptive trials, control allocation is often fixed (for example, 20% of the total sample), whereas allocation among experimental treatments is adjusted. All adaptation rules must be prespecified in the protocol, and computer simulations must control the overall type I error rate so repeated interim analyses do not inflate false positives. Methodological and reporting guidance is available from Bhatt and Mehta (2016) and Pallmann et al. (2018).
I-SPY 2 is an adaptive breast-cancer RCT intended to identify treatments according to tumor molecular biomarkers. All patients receive standard neoadjuvant chemotherapy while five novel drugs, each added to standard therapy, are tested. After baseline biopsy, imaging, and blood tests, patients are randomized to drug groups and response is assessed. To obtain early information, investigators model the relationship between response and biomarkers, continually evaluate results, and use them to determine randomization probabilities. Using Bayesian adaptive randomization, a drug that performs well in participants with a particular biomarker is preferentially assigned to later participants with that biomarker. When the probability that a drug is effective in all patients becomes sufficiently low, it leaves the trial. At the end, drugs more effective than standard therapy and their corresponding biomarker profiles are tested in further phase III trials. This approach can rapidly evaluate new drugs, identify effective drugs and combinations, and identify breast-cancer subtypes likely to benefit; information from each patient informs subsequent allocation.
In neurosurgery, GBM-AGILE is a seamless phase II/III glioma platform similar to I-SPY 2. In the first stage, multiple experimental arms are compared with a common control, using biomarker-based adaptive randomization to evaluate effects on survival. Arms showing substantial effects enter the second stage, where a fixed randomization design confirms effectiveness. This platform can accelerate access to treatment and speed drug registration and regulatory review.

2.7.1 Basket trials
A drug with a clearly defined target can be regarded as a basket: studying different cancers carrying the same target gene in that basket is a basket trial. In essence, one drug is tested across different tumors. The crizotinib A8081013 trial (NCT01121588) is a basket trial including a range of malignancies. Basket trials targeting BRAF are also widely conducted. BRAF mutations have been detected in multiple myeloma, melanoma, ovarian cancer, colorectal cancer, thyroid cancer, choriocarcinoma, gastrointestinal tumors, lung cancer, craniopharyngioma, and other cancers.


2.7.2 Umbrella trials
One disease may be driven by different genes; lung cancer, for example, may be driven by KRAS, EGFR, or ALK. Different subtypes of the same disease are gathered beneath one umbrella and receive distinct precision therapies according to their target genes. The I-SPY 2 and GBM-AGILE studies described above are umbrella trials.

title: 2  Randomized Controlled Trials
section: 2.8 Interpreting negative randomized controlled trial results
text:
2.8 Interpreting negative randomized controlled trial results
Well-designed RCTs raise the level of evidence for clinical practice. It is common but unreasonable to classify a study as positive or negative solely according to whether its p value is below 0.05. A p value should instead be understood as continuous: smaller values provide stronger evidence for a treatment effect. Confidence intervals estimate the range of uncertainty around the effect. Interpretation should also consider the totality of evidence—primary, secondary, and safety outcomes—not just the primary endpoint.
Earlier evidence suggests that only 13.8% of new-drug clinical studies initiated by pharmaceutical companies ultimately receive approval (Wong et al. 2019). Negative trials understandably disappoint patients and manufacturers. In neurosurgical trials, failure can reflect biological properties of drugs or characteristics of disease, including pharmacokinetic issues, lack of reliable animal models, and the blood–brain barrier. However, negative results can also reflect poor design. Resource-constrained investigator-initiated trials sometimes have design flaws that lead to negative conclusions; avoiding such deficiencies is essential for future RCTs.
According to their hypothesis, RCTs may be superiority, noninferiority, or equivalence trials; according to their randomization unit, they may be ordinary, cluster, or crossover trials. Consider a study assessing the safety of withholding perioperative corticosteroids for pituitary tumors. Its primary hypothesis is that withholding corticosteroids does not cause more complications than using them; a noninferiority design is therefore more appropriate, but was not used. Another advantage of noninferiority design is substantially smaller sample size and greater efficiency. If postoperative adrenal insufficiency is expected in 5% of the corticosteroid group and 10% of the no-corticosteroid group, a superiority design would require 864 participants, whereas a noninferiority design would require only 118. Randomization was another potential limitation. If two participants are enrolled in the same ward on the same day, inadequate procedures or staffing may lead to corticosteroids being given to a participant assigned not to receive them—effectively switching groups. Cluster randomization can avoid this problem. The cluster is often a health-care institution, ward, or time period, so these units are randomized. It can improve adherence because nearby patients generally receive the same regimen, management is more uniform, and contamination between groups is reduced.
The population studied also matters because sensitivity to treatment may vary. CRASH-3 evaluated tranexamic acid in all types of traumatic brain injury with mortality as the endpoint. Mortality was 18.5% with tranexamic acid and 19.8% with placebo, with a risk ratio of 0.94 (95% CI 0.86–1.02; p > 0.05), a result that could be labeled negative. Stratified analyses showed different effects: in mild-to-moderate injury the risk ratio was 0.78 (95% CI 0.64–0.95), whereas in severe injury it was 0.99 (95% CI 0.91–1.07). The study therefore concluded that tranexamic acid may reduce mortality in mild-to-moderate injury. In STICH-I, surgery versus conservative treatment for spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage did not differ on the primary endpoint, but subgroup analysis suggested better outcomes from early surgery in superficial cortical hematomas. STICH-II then studied superficial hematomas but likewise did not confirm surgical superiority; its subgroup analyses also suggested population heterogeneity, with patients of better prognosis possibly benefiting more from surgery. In EORTC 22033-26033, temozolomide versus radiotherapy for high-risk low-grade glioma was not positive in the overall population, but progression-free survival was longer with radiotherapy in the IDH-mutant/non-codeleted subgroup. Subgroup analysis is discussed further in Chapter 3.
Secondary outcomes can sometimes assist clinical decisions. In MISTIE-III, mortality was a secondary endpoint and was significantly lower with minimally invasive treatment than with conservative treatment, suggesting that minimally invasive treatment may reduce mortality in spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage. Both subgroup and secondary-outcome findings, however, require caution when interpreting results or guiding decisions: they involve multiple comparisons and have a greater probability of type I error and false-positive findings.
Because of type I error constraints, RCTs often include only one primary endpoint. Some neurosurgical diseases have clear endpoints, such as survival in glioma or endocrine control in functioning pituitary tumors. For traumatic brain injury and hemorrhagic disease, however, functional status may be assessed by several scales, including the modified Rankin Scale (mRS) and Glasgow Outcome Scale (GOS), and different cut-points may be considered. A trial comparing decompressive craniectomy with conservative treatment for traumatic intracranial hypertension used GOS as its primary endpoint. An exploratory dichotomized analysis using severe upper-limb paresis or better as the cut-point did not show a statistically significant difference, so strictly speaking the trial was negative. Yet the GOS distribution showed that decompressive craniectomy significantly reduced mortality (26.9% versus 48.9%; p < 0.05). Moreover, when outcomes are repeatedly measured events, such as endocrine remission in trials of functioning pituitary tumors, conventional designs often use only the first event and ignore later events. Recent studies suggest that including repeatedly measured outcomes can improve power.
RCTs must also consider participant adherence, adherence by treatment providers, and protocol deviations. MISTIE-III enrolled 506 adults with spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage and assessed neurologic status at 365 days, defining mRS 0–3 as a good outcome and 4–6 as a poor outcome. It found no evidence that minimally invasive surgery improved neurologic status versus conservative treatment. However, only 59% of participants achieved the target hematoma reduction (at least 15 mL), and earlier research showed a positive relation between evacuation volume and outcome. Treatment crossover is uncommon in blinded drug/placebo trials, but is a major issue in surgery/non-surgery trials. In STICH-II, although 294 participants were randomized to conservative treatment, 62 switched to surgery after randomization—a crossover rate of 21%.
Because negative results are defined statistically, statistical non-significance does not necessarily mean clinical irrelevance. In Corti-TC, hydrocortisone or fludrocortisone versus placebo did not statistically reduce hospital-acquired pneumonia after traumatic brain injury (risk ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.55–1.03; p > 0.05). Nevertheless, a potential 25% risk reduction may be clinically important. In CeTeG/NOA-09, lomustine plus temozolomide versus temozolomide alone for MGMT-positive glioma had median survival as the primary endpoint and a hazard ratio of 0.60 (95% CI 0.35–1.03; p > 0.05), conventionally a negative result. Yet median survival was 48.1 months with combination treatment versus 31.4 months with temozolomide alone, an average increase of 17 months that is clinically meaningful.
After a negative trial, investigators should also ask whether the sample size was adequate. In Corti-TC, hospital-acquired pneumonia in the placebo group was much less frequent than anticipated, meaning more participants were actually needed to detect a difference. Another study compared minimally invasive neurosurgery with conservative treatment for intracerebral hemorrhage. Thirty-day mortality was 9.5% with minimally invasive treatment and 14.8% with conservative treatment; although the difference was not statistically significant, the total sample was only 96, far below the planned size.
Finally, intention-to-treat analysis is the principal method in almost all RCTs: every randomized participant is analyzed regardless of subsequent events. A negative intention-to-treat result can, however, arise when some participants deviate from protocol. Per-protocol analyses are now often presented as subsequent exploratory analyses in high-quality RCTs. In CeTeG/NOA-09, some centers showed selection bias; an exploratory analysis excluded these centers and used inverse-probability weighting to control confounding, suggesting that lomustine plus temozolomide may perform better. Per-protocol analyses can nevertheless remain biased in the presence of unmeasured confounding.

title: 3  Statistical Considerations in Randomized Controlled Trials
text:
3.1 Intention-to-treat and per-protocol analysis
The analysis strategy usually used in randomized controlled trials is intention-to-treat (ITT): regardless of what happens after randomization, every randomized participant is analyzed in the group to which they were originally assigned. Per-protocol (PP) analysis instead analyzes enrolled participants according to their actual adherence to the protocol. Three misunderstandings about ITT are common.
First, ITT is not necessarily more likely than PP to show no effect. Suppose interventions A and B have the same biological effect. If A has more adverse effects and poorer adherence, while B has fewer adverse effects and better adherence, ITT may show that B is superior to A. Second, ITT is not inherently more conservative. If A causes more adverse effects, its participants may adhere less, so the adverse effects actually observed in A can resemble those in B. ITT may then conclude that adverse effects do not differ, even though more A participants deviated from protocol; that cannot simply be called more conservative. Third, ITT does not automatically reflect the real world better. When a couple asks a physician about the effectiveness of contraception, the useful answer is usually its effectiveness when used correctly—the PP result—not the ITT result under which 40% used it incorrectly.
Because of randomization, ITT can directly compare treatment groups. In PP analysis, however, groups can differ not only before randomization but also after randomization because of actual treatment received—for example, dose adjustments based on patient condition or loss to follow-up caused by adverse effects. PP analysis in an RCT therefore requires adjustment for pre- and post-randomization confounding, just as in a non-randomized study. The protocol should prespecify which post-randomization prognostic factors will be collected and how PP analysis will be performed.
In the causal language of Chapter 1, ITT estimates the causal effect of being assigned to an intervention—the assignment effect. It answers a policy-level question and is directly identifiable because of randomization. PP analysis estimates the effect of actually receiving intervention according to protocol. Because adherence is often affected by post-randomization prognostic factors, naive PP analysis creates selection bias and requires adjustment for post-randomization confounding, for example inverse-probability weighting (Hernán and Hernández-Díaz 2012).

title: 3  Statistical Considerations in Randomized Controlled Trials
text:
3.2 Protocol deviations
Two common types of protocol deviation are ineligibility and nonadherence.

3.2.1 Failure to meet eligibility criteria
Participants may violate eligibility criteria at enrollment because of documentation errors, laboratory errors, or misclassification. In a multicenter myocardial-infarction study, for example, participants admitted with possible acute myocardial infarction received intervention or placebo, but diagnosis was confirmed only after several days of electrocardiographic and serum-enzyme monitoring. Some were randomized on the basis of an initial diagnosis that later enzyme monitoring did not support.
A more complicated problem arises when the intervention itself affects eligibility. If it limits infarct size, it can change electrocardiographic and enzyme findings and thus affect diagnosis; this cannot occur in the placebo group. Ineligible control participants are easy to recognize, whereas truly ineligible intervention participants must be distinguished from those who merely appear ineligible because treatment worked. Three strategies are possible: do not enroll until diagnosis is confirmed and carefully checked; if ineligible participants must be removed, use only information collected before enrollment and have the decision-maker blinded to outcomes and allocation; or allow enrollment but do not remove them, since both groups have equal opportunity to include ineligible participants, although they may dilute outcome differences.


3.2.2 Adherence
Nonadherence is another reason participants leave analysis; loss to follow-up is one form. It may result from adverse events in either group, loss of interest or perceived benefit, changes in underlying condition, or other causes. Nonadherence diminishes any benefit of intervention over control and therefore increases the sample size needed. If it is greater in one group and related to outcome, removal of nonadherent participants can introduce bias. The best strategy is to minimize nonadherence in trial design and use ITT results.
The definition of adherence also matters. It may be defined as the proportion of actual intervention received that matches the protocol. Drug/placebo trials should describe adherence separately in intervention and control groups. If intervention-group adherence is lower, broad clinical uptake may not be reasonable: an intervention may work, but have little value if most participants cannot tolerate it.

3.3 Multiple comparisons
Suppose Zhang San guesses the outcome of five coin tosses and is correct each time. The probability, if he is not cheating, is:
Equation 3.1 Probability of five consecutive correct guesses
\[0.5^5 \approx 0.03\]
But if 100 people each guess five tosses and only Li Si is correct five times, it is no longer sensible to conclude that Li Si cheated. The probability that at least one person is correct five times is:
Equation 3.2 Probability that at least one of 100 people guesses five tosses correctly
\[1-(1-1/32)^{100}=0.958\]

p_one <- 1 / 2^5                 # one person guesses 5 correctly
p_any <- 1 - (1 - p_one)^100     # at least one of 100 does so
c(one_person = p_one, `at_least_one_of_100` = p_any)

Hypothesis testing relies on the small-probability principle: a small-probability event is regarded as unlikely in one experiment. Multiple hypothesis tests in the same study are no longer one experiment. In 1992, Swedish investigators examined residents living within 300 m of high-voltage power lines and, over 25 years, compared rates of more than 800 diseases with residents farther away. Childhood leukemia appeared four times as frequent and prompted government action. With more than 800 comparisons, however, one or more diseases can easily appear increased by chance. Multiple testing has two distinct control targets: family-wise error rate (FWER), controlled by methods such as Bonferroni and Holm, and false discovery rate (FDR), the expected proportion of false positives among rejected hypotheses, controlled by Benjamini–Hochberg and less conservative in large exploratory testing. See Schulz and Grimes (2005) for a systematic discussion in RCTs.

3.3.1 Multiple primary efficacy outcomes
The usual solution is to select the most important outcome as primary and regard others as secondary, or to construct a composite primary outcome. If multiple primary outcomes are essential: (1) if all must be significant, alpha need not be adjusted; (2) if any one significant outcome establishes efficacy, alpha must be allocated across outcomes, often by importance or equally, with total no greater than alpha. A simple Bonferroni correction is
Equation 3.3 Bonferroni correction
\[\text{adjusted }\alpha=0.05/n\]
where n is the number of primary outcomes. Bonferroni is simple but conservative, especially for large n. (3) Outcomes can be ranked and tested sequentially: test the most important first, and test the next only after rejecting the preceding null hypothesis. If a prior test is not significant, stop all later tests. Alpha adjustment is not needed, but the order must be specified in the protocol before unblinding and must never be selected or changed afterward.


3.3.2 Comparisons among multiple groups
When groups have an ordered dose relationship, sequential comparisons with control from high to low dose can be used without alpha adjustment. When no dose ordering exists, alpha must be adjusted; for example, mutual comparisons among experimental, placebo, and active-control groups commonly use Bonferroni alpha/n, where n is the number of comparisons.


3.3.3 Composite outcomes
When a composite is formed by weighting components (such as a score) or by defining a combined outcome (such as major adverse cardiovascular events), components may be tested after a significant composite without alpha adjustment. If components are tested regardless of composite significance and any one significant component establishes efficacy, alpha must be adjusted.


3.3.4 A change in comparison type for the same primary outcome
A common approach is first to compare experimental and active-control groups for noninferiority and, only if noninferiority is established, test superiority. Alpha adjustment is not required.

title: 3  Statistical Considerations in Randomized Controlled Trials
text:
3.4 Interim analysis and alpha spending
An interim analysis assesses efficacy and safety between intervention and control groups before formal trial completion according to a prespecified statistical analysis plan. Because its number, method, and results affect interpretation, every interim analysis must be described in advance in the protocol. If a special circumstance prevents this, the interim-analysis plan must at least be completed and the protocol amended before final analysis.
Its three usual purposes are: timely safety monitoring, with early stopping when safety problems appear; early confirmation of efficacy, with stopping for efficacy or futility when prespecified criteria are met; and sample-size re-estimation when limited prior information yields inaccurate estimates of efficacy, safety, or power.
Most interim analyses aim to show efficacy and therefore must control false positives. Each interim analysis is a hypothesis test; using alpha = 0.05 each time increases the overall type I error. To keep the overall type I error at 0.05, each analysis must use adjusted alpha. Each interim look spends part of alpha: more interim analyses consume more alpha and leave less for the final analysis. The schedule, arrangements, and alpha allocation must be planned and stated in the protocol. Common approaches are Pocock, O’Brien–Fleming, and Peto boundaries. Pocock is simple: with one interim and one final analysis, alpha is 0.029 at both looks, but the final threshold is much smaller than 0.05. O’Brien–Fleming uses a stringent early threshold that relaxes as information accumulates; if the planned sample is reached, the final analysis is much like one without an interim look, while a strong advantage can still stop the trial early. Peto is similar but uses an especially small early threshold (0.001), making early stopping difficult. In the alpha-spending-function framework, alpha expenditure is prespecified as information accumulates, allowing flexible timing and number of looks (DeMets and Lan 1994).
Case 3.1
KEYNOTE-604 was a randomized, double-blind phase III study in which 453 eligible patients with lung cancer were randomized 1:1 to pembrolizumab or placebo for 35 cycles or until disease progression. Progression-free and overall survival were primary endpoints. Two interim analyses and one final analysis were planned, with alpha 0.0024, 0.0071, and 0.012, respectively. Neither interim analysis was positive. At final analysis, median overall survival was 10.8 versus 9.7 months, and the ITT comparison did not reach significance (hazard ratio 0.80; 95% CI 0.64–0.98; p = 0.016). Although survival curves separated, the small difference between 0.016 and 0.012 produced a negative result. Alpha spent in interim analyses cannot be ignored: without interim analyses, overall survival would have been positive. Clinicians need to understand these methods so that a clinically important difference is not declared negative because of an unsuitable statistical design or analysis.

title: 3  Statistical Considerations in Randomized Controlled Trials
text:
3.5 Subgroup analysis
Subgroup analysis groups participants by baseline characteristics to assess whether responses differ. It can support or clarify an overall effect and generate exploratory findings for a particular subgroup, but is often misleading. Subgroups should be prespecified: continued post-trial exploration will almost always find at least one suggestive subgroup effect. The protocol should state proposed subgroups and their biological rationale. Stratification factors such as age, sex, and disease stage are implicitly subgroups. Post hoc, data-mining analyses without biological rationale should primarily generate hypotheses for other trials.
Multiple-comparison adjustment is needed when many subgroups are tested, for example with Bonferroni or other methods, and apparently concentrated effects should be sought in a similar independent trial. Interaction tests, rather than separate within-subgroup treatment estimates, should be used: an interaction provides a global assessment of whether the subgroup variable relates to treatment effect, with estimates and confidence intervals. Separate subgroup tests require more hypotheses and inflate false positives. Differences observed between subgroups do not necessarily mean heterogeneous treatment effects, especially when the primary effect is non-significant. Wang et al. (2007) summarize the principles of prespecification, interaction testing, and multiplicity adjustment; Sun et al. (2010) provide practical credibility criteria including prespecification, interaction evidence, and replication.

title: 3  Statistical Considerations in Randomized Controlled Trials
text:
3.6 Multicenter clinical research
Multicenter trials are common because a single center rarely recruits enough participants. Analysis should consider center effects to understand the overall average effect, variation in treatment effect, and effects across centers. Randomization is usually stratified by center to balance treatment within each center.
One model omits center effects and treats all variation as participant-level variation, assuming no systematic differences among centers. A more appropriate model separates variation among participants within centers from variation among centers. Omitting center effects overestimates variability in the average treatment effect, produces wider confidence intervals, and reduces power. A model including center effects recognizes that part of variation reflects differences in populations treated at each center, reduces within-center residual variation, and increases precision. Center may be modeled as a fixed effect in linear models, survival analysis, or logistic regression, allowing outcomes within a center to resemble each other more than outcomes across centers.

section: 3.7 Appendix: Statistical reporting standards of the New England Journal of Medicine
text:
3.7 Appendix: Statistical reporting standards of the New England Journal of Medicine

3.7.1 All studies

The Methods section should describe sample-size and power considerations and briefly describe analyses of primary and secondary outcomes.
The Methods section should explain handling of missing data. Except when data are very sparse, complete-case analysis should not be primary analysis; use appropriate imputation based on the missing-data mechanism. Multiple imputation or inverse-probability weighting may be used for missing at random, whereas model-based approaches are more suitable for missing not at random.
Point estimates of effects, associations, and other parameters should be accompanied by confidence intervals adjusted according to alpha.
Unless design such as a noninferiority trial requires a one-sided test, reported p values should be two-sided. In general, report values above 0.01 to two decimals, 0.01–0.001 to three decimals, and values below 0.001 as p < 0.001. Prespecified stopping-rule and genome-wide association p values may use other precision.
Reported precision should not exceed that justified by scientific meaning and sample size; odds ratios generally use two decimals.



3.7.2 Clinical trials

Submit original and final protocols, the statistical analysis plan, and a dated list of protocol amendments.
Analyze the primary outcome as prespecified. Explain analyses not in the original protocol; editors may request additional analyses.
Use the protocol-specified procedure to control overall type I error for comparisons. Prespecified exploratory analyses should use the stated method, for example Benjamini–Hochberg for FDR.
Without a prespecified multiplicity-control method, secondary and exploratory endpoints should be limited to point estimates and 95% confidence intervals. State that interval widths are not multiplicity-adjusted, that inferences may not replicate, and do not report p values.
Prespecified subgroup analyses should follow the protocol. Important post hoc analyses require justification and clear labeling. Forest plots are useful for showing estimates in important subgroups; multiple interaction p values have limited inferential value and ordinarily should not be provided.
Safety outcomes that are not primary endpoints need not be multiplicity-adjusted when significance tests are reported, because a larger type I error is acceptable for safety information.
Before risk differences or risk ratios, report absolute event counts or rates; avoid odds ratios when they can overstate relative risk or be misinterpreted.
Provide a CONSORT flow diagram and all relevant CONSORT checklist information.



3.7.3 Observational studies

Validity depends on sample selection, measured and unmeasured confounding, and methods of controlling confounding; explain how these issues were handled in design and analysis.
Submit a signed and dated prespecified statistical analysis plan when one exists.
For multiple tests, use a prespecified type I error-control method. Without one, limit statistics to point estimates and 95% confidence intervals, state that intervals are not multiplicity-adjusted and may not replicate, and do not report p values.
List planned analyses, inclusion criteria, and data-sampling methods, with figures or tables where appropriate; identify the association or causal relationship to be estimated and why.
Studies reporting treatment effects should show distributions of potential confounders and other variables between treatment groups.
Explain complex models in a supplement where possible; use sensitivity analysis to discuss bias from unmeasured confounding, or explicitly discuss it if sensitivity analysis was not done.
Replicate findings in one or more similar independent studies to assess robustness.

title: 4  Writing Randomized Controlled Trial Protocols and Informed Consent
text:
4.1 Writing an RCT protocol
Writing a protocol and participant informed-consent materials is an important step before conducting an RCT. This chapter sets out the key elements and provides a model protocol. Protocols should follow the SPIRIT 2013 statement (Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials), which provides a 33-item checklist. A trial should also be prospectively registered on a public registry, such as ClinicalTrials.gov or the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry, before participant enrollment (Chan et al. 2013).

title: 4  Writing Randomized Controlled Trial Protocols and Informed Consent
text:
4.1.1 1. Research background
The protocol should provide sufficient background to demonstrate the importance and necessity of the question, expected benefits, and relevant references and data. It should describe prior laboratory and animal research, scientific literature, and other information supporting the rationale; it should summarize domestic and international progress and identify the innovation of the proposed study.
A useful sequence is: define the research question; describe the current situation and its deficiencies; review relevant domestic and international progress; explain what the study will do, its innovations, and its clinical or societal value; describe prior work and the conditions supporting the scientific rationale, feasibility, and regulatory compliance; and assess possible risks, the justification for choosing the population, potential benefit, and whether benefit outweighs risk.


4.1.2 2. Objectives
Every study needs clear objectives: the question it will answer or problem it will solve. In drug research, objectives generally concern safety and efficacy. Too many objectives make data collection and analysis more complex and can compromise feasibility.


4.1.3 3. Design, randomization, and blinding
The protocol should state how the allocation sequence will be generated, for example by computer-generated random numbers; how the sequence will be implemented, for example through a central telephone system; and how it will be kept unknown before allocation. It should confirm clinical equipoise—the genuine uncertainty about comparative treatment effects that makes random allocation ethically acceptable.
Blinding can reduce measurement bias. State who will be blinded (participants, investigators, outcome assessors), whether the study is single- or double-blind, and how blinding will be implemented. For an unblinded study, explain why and describe bias-control measures. Specify unblinding procedures and emergency code-breaking arrangements.


4.1.4 4. Inclusion, exclusion, withdrawal, and stopping criteria
Inclusion and exclusion criteria usually address demographic information (age, sex, race), health and disease requirements, concomitant medication, previous treatment, and other relevant factors. Disease and severity requirements should use recognized diagnostic standards rather than standards altered to suit the study, because the latter harms reliability. In addition to the target indication, consider whether study procedures or interventions could harm patients of a given severity and whether risks are controllable. Restrictions on comorbidities, behavior, and lifestyle (such as smoking or alcohol) can control confounding, clarify treatment effects, and reduce unexpected serious adverse events; too many restrictions make the sample unrepresentative and limit generalizability.
For safety, participants normally may not join more than one clinical study at a time. Specify a washout period after prior drug trials. People of reproductive potential generally need effective contraception during the study. If mutagenic or reproductive toxicity in men cannot be excluded, male participants should also use effective contraception.
Specify when a participant must stop treatment or leave the study, rather than when the whole project stops: unwillingness or inability to continue; discovery after enrollment that eligibility is not met; intolerable adverse events or serious adverse events for which continued participation has more risk than benefit; no improvement or deterioration after continuous treatment (with a defined time point for judging ineffectiveness); loss to follow-up; or use of protocol-prohibited drugs or treatments. Specify criteria for stopping the entire study: major protocol errors or serious deviations that prevent assessment; treatment-related adverse events making continuation inappropriate; a requirement from regulators, government, or the ethics committee; or other situations in which investigators consider continuation unsuitable or impossible.


4.1.5 5. Sample size
Calculate the number of participants needed to achieve the objective using statistical principles. Consider the minimum clinically important difference, variability of the primary measure, type I error (alpha; false positive), type II error (beta; false negative), one- or two-sided testing, the statistical test, and expected loss to follow-up.


4.1.6 6. Study procedures
RCTs usually include screening, intervention, and follow-up periods. Describe all study content and steps in detail, preferably with a flowchart. State clinical and laboratory assessments, their frequency, volume and number of blood or tissue specimens, and total specimen volume. State the route, method, frequency, and duration of intervention. For drugs, specify formulation, dose, route, administration method, frequency, course, and rules for concomitant medication; also describe accountability, use records, delivery, dispensing, storage, packaging, and labeling. Specify follow-up visits and content, and measures to support adherence, such as diary cards, adherence education, pill counts, and return of drug containers.
For drug interventions, specify rules for stopping, reducing, and resuming dose after adverse drug reactions, how reactions will be managed, how loss to follow-up is defined, and the process that follows it.


4.1.7 7. Efficacy assessment
Studies assessing efficacy require outcome measures. There may be primary and secondary outcomes, each with standards for measurement method, observation time, recording, and analysis.


4.1.8 8. Adverse events
Record in detail every clinical adverse event and abnormal laboratory result, evaluate its relationship to the study drug, and judge severity. An adverse event is any unfavorable medical occurrence or clinically meaningful laboratory abnormality during a trial, whether or not related to study treatment. For each, describe onset, duration, management, outcome, severity, and relationship to study drug.
A serious adverse event (SAE) is any unfavorable event at any dose that results in death, is life-threatening, requires or prolongs hospitalization, causes persistent or substantial disability/incapacity, causes a congenital anomaly/birth defect, or is an important medical event that may jeopardize the participant or require intervention to prevent one of these outcomes. On an SAE, investigators should immediately protect the participant and report it to the ethics committee and relevant authorities within 24 hours.
Classify relationship according to temporal sequence, reaction type, and response to withdrawal/rechallenge as definitely related, probably related, possibly related, possibly unrelated, or definitely unrelated. “Definitely related” requires evidence of exposure, a reasonable time relationship, a more plausible drug explanation than alternatives, a positive dechallenge, and, where feasible, a positive rechallenge. “Probably related” has exposure, a reasonable time relationship, a more plausible drug explanation, and positive dechallenge. “Possibly related” has exposure and a reasonable temporal relationship but may have another explanation and positive dechallenge. “Possibly unrelated” is better explained by another cause, with negative or unclear dechallenge. “Definitely unrelated” involves no exposure, no temporal relationship, or another definite cause.


4.1.9 9. Other items
Address construction of electronic case-report forms or research records; data entry and amendment; confidentiality of participant information and research data; quality control and assurance; ethics; recruitment and the consent process; anticipated progress and completion date; responsibilities of all parties; and other relevant rules.

4.2 Writing participant informed consent

State that the participant is being invited to clinical research and that participation is voluntary.
Describe national and international progress concerning the intervention.
Introduce the design, including blinding, control, or crossover, and the planned number of participants.
Describe the main content, procedures and duration, number of follow-ups, tests or procedures and their frequency, possible allocation to different groups, and medication methods.
Explain known and unknown adverse reactions and possible risks and discomfort from study procedures.
Explain potential benefits, such as curing disease or preventing/slowing progression, or clearly state that there may be no direct benefit; describe alternative therapies outside the study.
Explain whether intervention and examination costs are waived, whether travel reimbursement is available, and whether free treatment and compensation are available for study-related injury.
Explain participant responsibilities and rights, including the right to decline or withdraw at any time after notifying the investigator, and confidentiality of personal information. The entire consent process must comply with the Declaration of Helsinki, ICH Good Clinical Practice (ICH-GCP), and China’s GCP ethics requirements. Consent must contain all these elements, be written in language the participant can understand, and be signed voluntarily after adequate information and without coercion (World Medical Association 2013).

4.3 Appendix: Protocol for a prospective multicenter study of drug A combined with radiotherapy for disease B

4.3.1 Contents and protocol synopsis
Contents and protocol synopsis are omitted in this example. A trial flow chart should state the key treatment and follow-up time points during the study.


4.3.2 Background

4.3.2.1 1. Introduction to disease B
(Omitted.)


4.3.2.2 2. Summary of radiotherapy for disease B
The main purpose of radiotherapy is to prevent tumor growth. All patients with disease B whose imaging suggests residual tumor should be considered for radiotherapy. Evidence is limited, but conventionally fractionated external-beam radiotherapy and stereotactic radiotherapy can both control tumor growth. Conventional external-beam radiotherapy usually totals 45–54 Gy in 25–30 fractions and is mainly used for irregular tumors; stereotactic radiotherapy may be selected when tumor invasion involves important structures. No randomized comparison is available, but increasing reports suggest that radiotherapy may control growth.


4.3.2.3 3. Summary of drug A for disease B
Drug A is a novel alkylating agent for malignant tumors. It is widely distributed without hepatic or renal metabolism, rapidly crosses the blood–brain barrier, enters cerebrospinal fluid, and reaches effective concentrations in the central nervous system. In 1999, it was first approved by the US FDA for recurrent or progressive malignant tumors after standard therapy. Compared with radiotherapy alone, drug A plus radiotherapy can prolong overall and progression-free survival in malignant tumors.
Increasing reports suggest that drug A can control growth and reduce volume in disease B that is difficult to control with conventional treatment. Many reports from the United States, France, Japan, and elsewhere show response rates of 40%–70%. Overall, about 60% of patients have reduced tumor volume and substantial symptom relief after drug A, whereas about 40% are insensitive or develop chemotherapy resistance.

4.3.2.5 5. Proposed study
To further verify the efficacy and safety of drug A in disease B and compare radiotherapy alone with concurrent chemoradiotherapy, a multicenter study is planned to obtain more reliable and generalizable results. This prospective, multicenter, large-sample study will assess efficacy and safety of drug A plus radiotherapy in Chinese patients with disease B, standardize its use, reduce mortality and disability, and improve survival and quality of life.


4.3.2.6 6. Risk–benefit assessment
The risk–benefit assessment should summarize known and uncertain toxicities of drug A and radiotherapy, safety-monitoring procedures, alternatives, and the anticipated benefit to participants and society. Continuation requires that anticipated benefit outweigh reasonably foreseeable risk.



4.3.3 Objectives and endpoints
Specify the primary objective, safety objective, and exploratory objectives; define the primary and secondary endpoints, their measurement windows, and their analysis populations.


4.3.4 Study design
Specify the prospective multicenter randomized design, study sites, allocation ratio, allocation concealment, blinding where feasible, recruitment target, and planned duration.


4.3.5 Study treatment
Specify radiotherapy planning and delivery, the drug A regimen, concomitant treatments, dose modification and discontinuation rules, accountability, and adherence procedures.


4.3.6 Study procedures
The detailed intervention and examination schedule is omitted in this example. The protocol should identify baseline, treatment, and follow-up visits, required imaging, laboratory tests, efficacy evaluation, and safety assessments.


4.3.7 Study evaluation
Define efficacy, imaging, clinical, and quality-of-life evaluation standards, assessment intervals, and endpoint adjudication procedures.


4.3.8 Adverse events
For adverse-event procedures, see the adverse-event section of this chapter.


4.3.9 Data management
Specify eCRF completion, source-data verification, data query and correction, coding, database lock, access control, and confidentiality procedures.


4.3.10 Statistical analysis
Define analysis sets, sample-size justification, primary and secondary endpoint analyses, handling of missing data, subgroup and sensitivity analyses, and safety analyses.


4.3.11 Clinical monitoring
Specify monitoring frequency, responsibilities, source-data review, protocol-deviation reporting, and communication with investigators.


4.3.12 Quality assurance
Describe training, standard operating procedures, audits, quality-control checks, and corrective and preventive actions.


4.3.13 Handling unusual events during the trial
State procedures for protocol deviations, emergency unblinding, pregnancy, loss to follow-up, product complaints, regulatory reporting, suspension, and early termination.


4.3.14 Insurance and compensation
State insurance coverage and the arrangements for medical care and compensation for study-related injury.
